title: "Synthesis and Conclusion"

## Closing the Research Gap

<!-- Rehash intro and motivation and then summarise how each chapter links to the research gaps/questions/objectives. -->
Needleleaf forest canopies can intercept a large fraction of snowfall and alter the phase, timing, and quantity of precipitation reaching the ground. In cold continental climates, up to half of annual snowfall may be lost to the atmosphere via canopy snow sublimation, and in warmer climates, higher melt rates cause a large fraction of snowfall to reach the ground as liquid. Sparse observations of canopy snow processes and forest snow accumulation—primarily located in cold continental climates or warm maritime climates with dense forest canopies—have led to process representations that have uncertain extrapolation across the globe. Existing theories and resulting parameterisations commonly used in hydrological and land-surface models to represent snow interception and canopy snow ablation include: observations from cold-continental boreal forests for interception and unloading [@Hedstrom1998; @Ellis2010] and sublimation of intercepted snow [@Pomeroy1998b]; observations from warm maritime climates for interception and unloading [@Storck2002; @Andreadis2009]; and an unloading model based on indirect measurements of canopy snow ablation at several sites [@Roesch2001]. Snow interception and canopy snow ablation processes exhibit a strong dependence on both meteorology and canopy density, leading to differing process emergence in existing theories developed in these distinct environments and limited transferability to new regions. Differing methodologies used to develop existing theories have also introduced uncertainty regarding the extent to which snow interception and canopy snow ablation processes are captured, leading to further differences in processes represented by current models. As a result, existing models exhibit high variability and uncertainty in predicting land-surface albedo, snow accumulation, melt, and subsequent runoff or infiltration in forested snow-dominated basin. Moreover, as the global climate warms there is a need to ensure existing theories to represent snow interception processes are robust across a range of meteorological conditions and evolving forests. The aim of this research was to evaluate the suitability of existing theories of snow interception and canopy snow ablation on their transferability across a wide range of climate and forest types. This thesis also links this improved process understanding to model development and validation to test new theories across a range of climate and forest types.

In @sec-chapter-2, a comprehensive literature review was conducted to establish major gaps in the literature. In this review the theories and assumptions underpinning existing snow interception and canopy snow ablation parameterisations are presented. Through this review it was revealed that there has been limited research on the transferability of existing parameterisations across a range of canopy densities or meteorological conditions. Moreover, existing discussions of differing process behaviour and emergence in existing models is typically equated to differing environmental conditions in previous studies. However, this work outlines that differing methodological approaches for measuring individual processes also contributes to the differing relationships that have been developed. Existing theories of initial interception [@Satterlund1967; @Schmidt1991; @Hedstrom1998], represent a strong increase in throughfall with increasing canopy snow load and air temperature. However, the long duration of snowfall events [@Hedstrom1998; @Schmid1997] and temperatures occasionally near the melting point [@Satterlund1967] greatly increased the probability of unloading within these measurements. This mixing of processes in measurements and resulting parameterisations introduces potential double counting of processes in hydrological models if these initial interception parameterisations were also combined with comprehensive canopy snow unloading routines. It was also identified that previous snow interception parameterisations were developed on small spatial scales such as point [@Storck2002] or transect [@Hedstrom1998] in distinctive climates, thus adding uncertainty to their transferability across diverse canopy structures over larger scales. Therefore, it was determined that additional observations of throughfall and snow interception are needed that minimize the inclusion of ablation processes, and span a gradient of meteorological conditions and canopy densities. In addition to these gaps regarding the initial interception process, canopy snow unloading measurements are reported by several studies to be difficult to collect due to their simultaneous occurrence with other ablation processes and has led to limited and sparse measurements. As a result, existing dry-snow unloading parameterisations are based on indirect measurements of canopy snow unloading such as changes in above canopy albedo [@Roesch2001; @Bartlett2015] which may also incorporate other ablation processes than unloading (i.e., sublimation losses). Moreover, differentiating between ablation of canopy snow as solid (unloading) and liquid (drip) during unloading is also reported as a challenge in the literature due to freeze-thaw processes that impact instrument functionality. Thus, resulting parameterisations to represent the partitioning of canopy snow into liquid meltwater and solid snow unloading are based on limited observations from limited events from two sites [@Storck2002; @Floyd2012]. To address this research gap, additional direct measurements of canopy snow unloading and drip were identified as necessary, alongside hybrid approaches to differentiate processes when they cannot be measured. An overarching theme from this review is the need to rigorously evaluate the theories underlying existing parameterisations using observations that isolate individual processes within the canopy snow mass and energy balance.

@sec-chapter-3 aimed to address several research gaps regarding process understanding of initial interception of snow in needleleaf canopies across a broad range in canopy density and meteorologies. The study assessed relationships between initial interception, canopy snow load, meteorology, and canopy density using observations that limited the effect of canopy snow ablation processes. The first research gap this study addressed was that established theories regarding maximum canopy snow load capacity and the influence of air temperature on initial interception [@Hedstrom1998; @Storck2002; @Andreadis2009; @Ellis2010] were not confirmed at this study site. This discrepancy is likely because earlier studies incorporated unloading processes within their interception measurements. It was hypothesised that branch compression, influenced by both air temperature and canopy snow load, together with the expansion of contact area as snow bridged canopy gaps and variations in snow adhesion and cohesion, offset these opposing relationships with interception, thereby limiting their detection in this study. A second research gap this chapter addressed was to investigate the relationship of initial snow interception across a broad range in canopy densities. In a subalpine forest with variable canopy density, it was found interception efficiency before ablation could be predicted by snow-leaf contact area which is moderated by canopy coverage and hydrometeor trajectory angle—estimated as a function of wind speed and hydrometeor velocity. An existing relationship [@Hedstrom1998] to describe the change in leaf-contact area with hydrometeor trajectory angle was not confirmed by observations collected in this study. The invalidation of existing interception theory assumptions—particularly regarding maximum canopy snow load and air temperature—combined with newly identified relationships between interception and leaf contact area, provided motivation for the development of two improved parameterisations for initial interception. The first parameterisation approximates snow-leaf contact area using wind speed, hydrometeor velocity, and nadir canopy cover. The second parameterisation, similar to rainfall interception models, calculates initial interception as a function of leaf contact area. This approach improved the prediction of throughfall of snow across a broad range in canopy densities and meteorological conditions. By minimizing ablation in the initial interception measurements, this model is expected to be more compatible with canopy snow ablation parameterisations that include a comprehensive representation of unloading, melt/drip, and sublimation processes.

In @sec-chapter-4 new observations of canopy snow ablation were presented—collected over events with meteorological conditions representative of climates ranging from the cold boreal forest to temperate maritime—and provided new insights on processes governing unloading and melt/drip of intercepted snow. The direct measurements of canopy snow unloading presented here provide an important contribution to the literature as previous studies typically relied on in-direct observations of dry snow unloading [@Roesch2001; @Bartlett2015] to develop parameterisations and may have been influenced by other processes than unloading (e.g., above canopy albedo is influenced by unloading, melt, and sublimation). Moreover, observations of melt-induced unloading were previously limited to two sites [@Storck2002; @Floyd2012] with limited variability in canopy snow loads. These new observations identified canopy snow load, wind shear stress, and the canopy snowmelt rate as primary predictors of unloading. These results align with previous studies emphasizing the importance of representing both cold/dry and melt-induced unloading processes. However, the relationships observed here incorporated predictors with stronger physical foundations. For example, using wind shear stress provided improved predictive power than wind speed, likely due to its more direct representation of the mechanical forces acting on intercepted snow. Similarly, a physically based energy balance approach to melt and unload canopy snow offered improved performance compared to temperature index models [@Ellis2010; @Roesch2001]. In addition, a new linear relationship was identified, showing that the amount of solid snow unloading during melt events increased proportionally with canopy snow load. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of representing both dry and melt-induced unloading and prioritizing physically based methods. They also provide new context for the maximum canopy snow load used in previous interception and ablation models, demonstrating that unloading increases proportionally with canopy snow load rather than after reaching a fixed threshold. Moreover, given the strong dependence of unloading on canopy load, the weak influence of canopy snow load on throughfall observed in @sec-chapter-3 may be explained as unloading occurs before canopy coverage can be substantially modified. 

In @sec-chapter-5 new parameterisations to represent the mass and energy balance of snow intercepted in the canopy—developed in Chapters 3 and 4—were incorporated as a new module in CRHM. An evaluation of the quantity and duration of SWE intercepted in the canopy was found to improve at one site where snow load observations were available. The updated model also resulted in substantial reduction in simulated SWE error at the warm-humid Russell Creek site due to the better physical representation of the canopy snowmelt, drip, and unloading representation compared to an existing model. The reduction in error by the new model was smaller at the three cold climate sites (Fortress, Marmot, and Wolf Creek), however, there is a large difference in the amount and duration of snow load intercepted in the canopy. Although the net quantity of snow/meltwater reaching the ground was relatively similar in the three colder climate sites between the two models the large difference in simulated canopy snow load has implications for surface albedo representation in land-surface schemes. The results presented here suggest improved transferability of forest-snow interaction models across diverse canopy structures and climates. These results also highlight the strong dependence of forest-snow interactions on both climate and canopy structure resulting in a large variability in the quantity and phase of snowfall reaching the ground across all sites. At two lower snowfall sites with calm winds and cold temperatures, roughly half of annual snowfall was lost to the atmosphere via sublimation due to lower canopy snow loads and wind-induced unloading resulting in reduced canopy snow unloading rates. A site with higher wind speed and cold temperatures, resulted in higher unloading rates which in turn reduced canopy snow sublimation. Russell Creek had nearly half of annual snowfall melt in the canopy due to warm temperatures and high humidity. This high melt rate, coupled with increased melt-induced unloading rates and reduced vapour pressure deficit, led to very low sublimation losses. Across the four sites, climate and canopy density were found to be more important drivers for influencing snow interception and subsequent canopy snow ablation processes than species-level differences among fir- and spruce-dominated forests.

## How Does This Work Advance the Discipline?

### Process-based Diagnosis of Theory

Many advances in hydrology have arisen from empirically diagnosing individual processes to improve their representation in hydrological models [e.g., @Pomeroy1993; @Pradhananga2022; @Gray1985; @Ireson2022]. The robustness of such parameterisations depends on the quality of the underlying observations, making detailed measurements essential. This thesis placed particular emphasis on constructing a methodological framework focused on the careful collection of observations to enable a process-based analysis which has previously been limited by previous measurement methodologies. As a result, throughfall/interception measurements could be better isolated from unloading/ablation processes contributing to an assessment of snow interception relationships that better reflects the individual process. These process measurements were also collected across varying canopy densities and meteorological conditions providing an evaluation of relationships across diverse conditions compared to existing studies which focused only on dense forest canopies in cold-continental [@Hedstrom1998] and warm-maritime [@Storck2002] climates. New advances in aerial lidar technology allow the collection of canopy density and structure measurements over large areas [@Staines2023; @Moeser2015b; @Roth2019], however corresponding process measurements at matching high resolution (i.e., throughfall) have been limited. This thesis provides the first linkage between high resolution throughfall observations and canopy structure derived from aerial lidar while also integrating subcanopy lysimeter measurements of throughfall and unloading at a high temporal frequency, allowing for the evaluation of theory across a broad range in canopy densities and meteorologies.

### Advancing Theories of Snowfall Partitioning by Forest Canopies 

In addition to the evaluation of existing theories with field measurements, this thesis developed a comprehensive framework that connects new insights on canopy snow processes to both process understanding and practical steps for overcoming limitations of current approaches in hydrological models. New parameterisations were introduced to represent snow interception and canopy snow ablation processes which demonstrated improved accuracy in representing canopy snow load and subcanopy snow accumulation across diverse forest and climate types. By more explicitly representing the underlying physical processes, these parameterisations reduce the danger of approximating the right answer for the wrong reason and enhance the potential for transferability to new sites.

The new relationships revealed through this work highlight the variability of snow interception processes in sparse forest canopies across varying canopy densities. It was shown this variability could be represented using commonly available input data (wind speed, canopy cover, and hydrometeor fall velocity) across a wide range of meteorological conditions. However, most hydrological and land surface models classify land cover into broad forested and non-forested categories, failing to capture the heterogeneity of snow processes in these environments. Results from this thesis demonstrate that interception efficiency can vary by a factor of two in sparse canopies with wind speeds from 0 to 1 m s^-1^—variability that mosaic/binary land cover partitioning cannot resolve. This finding highlights the importance of treating forests as a continuous distribution of canopy densities in order to more accurately represent the variability of possible interception efficiencies in these diverse forests. The revised approach not only advances representation of snow accumulation in forests but also aligns more closely with the rainfall interception literature, providing a more consistent and transferable framework for hydrological and land surface model development.

New relationships building on new observations and existing theories were developed to represent canopy snow unloading and melt, resulting in improved estimates of subcanopy SWE, canopy snow load, canopy snow cover duration, and individual processes (sublimation, unloading, and melt/drip). These advances highlight the importance of a comprehensive coupled representation of the canopy snow mass and energy balance. Parameters for initial interception and unloading are now more directly linked to the processes they represent, improving the clarity and interpretability of model calculations. Collectively, the new parameterisations better capture individual forest-snow processes and demonstrate stronger transferability across sites and under future climate conditions.

### Model Framework for Understanding Changes to Snow Storage in Forested Basins

These results provide new a diagnostic framework to investigate how climate and vegetation change will alter snowfall partitioning by needleleaf canopies, and have the potential to increase understanding of implications on downstream water resources. Both observations and simulations from this research demonstrate that snowfall partitioning varies substantially with climatic regime and canopy density. The improved transferability of parameterisations across diverse climate and forest types strengthens confidence in using this new model to diagnose future changes in forested basin snow storage under climate warming and vegetation shifts. These findings also highlight the risks of extrapolating snow storage estimates from open sites to forested areas in an evolving environment. As temperatures rise, canopy snow regimes may transition from sublimation-dominated processes to melt-dominated ones, altering both the timing and quantity of snow reaching the ground thus changing relationships between snow storage in open environments and total basin snow water storage. The parameterisations and model framework developed in this thesis provide tools to diagnose and predict such transitions, with direct implications for snow hydrology in forested basins and for land surface modelling schemes due to the influence of canopy snow coverage on albedo.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Future work is needed to continue to improve our understanding of how snowfall is partitioned by needleleaf canopies and to mobilise these findings into decision-making tools for managing water resources in snow-dominated forested basins. The empirical coefficients developed to represent initial interception, canopy density, and unloading require further validation across differing climatic conditions and forest compositions of varying species and ages. While these coefficients could be calibrated to reduce errors in subcanopy SWE or streamflow, this risks model equifinality—producing correct outputs through incorrect process representation [@Beven2006a]—as seen in pre-existing models. A more robust approach, as demonstrated in this thesis, constrain parameters using process-level observations of the corresponding process. This method could be extended to determine appropriate parameter ranges using similar observations to those collected in this thesis across various forest types, structures, and climates.

This study focused on forests composed of needleleaf species (e.g., pine, spruce, and fir); consequently, the applicability of the theoretical framework and associated empirical coefficients to forests of different ages or to species with alternative leaf structures—such as scale-leaved western red cedar (*Thuja plicata*) or broadleaf canopies, including structurally distinct canopies in the Southern Hemisphere [e.g., @Huerta2019]—remains untested. A fundamental difference may occur in broadleaf canopies where the shape of individual trees may result in a differing relationship of snow-leaf contact area with hydrometeor trajectory angle, compared to the coniferous trees observed in this study [@Herwitz1995]. Although cohesion and adhesion forces showed minimal variation in this study, their known temperature dependence warrants investigation into whether explicitly representing these processes improves interception efficiency calculations in other environments [@Kobayashi1987; @Pfister1999]. Additionally, the species-specific canopy load capacities used in previous models [@Andreadis2009; @Hedstrom1998] likely relate to the unloading rate coefficients presented here. These parameters may implicitly capture differences in branch rigidity and size associated with species, age, and temperature—factors that influence branch deformation under increasing snow load and, in turn, affect unloading rates and their relationship with snow load. Moreover, rainfall interception studies have demonstrated that liquid water storage capacity varies with tree age class [e.g., @Pypker2005a] and species [e.g., @Xiao2016], implying that canopy snow unloading rates may also differ across age classes. The canopy snow ablation measurements presented here were limited to four lysimeters installed within a mixed fir and spruce forest plot and thus limited interpretation on how varied species and forest structure/density influences canopy snow ablation could be ascertained from these datasets. Moreover, validation of snow load, canopy ablation, and snow-covered duration relied on weighed trees that were mature (~10 m) fir and spruce. Consequently, the transferability of these results to forests dominated by younger trees or species with more flexible and less supportive branch structures (e.g., cedar, hemlock) remains uncertain. Future research should collect observations across a wider range of species, ages, and canopy densities to better constrain estimates of interception and unloading coefficients.

The new canopy snow model requires estimates of within-canopy wind flow to calculate interception and energy balance parameterisations, as well as within-canopy shear stress to simulate wind-driven unloading. While site-specific observations enabled robust model development at Fortress (@sec-chapter-3; @sec-chapter-4), the reliance on simplified parameterisations in @sec-appdx-ch5 constrained model performance when applied at other sites. Future improvements could be achieved through more physically based representations of within-canopy wind flow that explicitly account for forest structural characteristics and variations in air density [@Stull2017].

A key process that is likely important to represent in more transitional or maritime climates is the accumulation of ice in the canopy through freeze-thaw cycles, freezing rain, frost deposition, and rime accretion [@Berndt1969; @Lumbrazo2022]. These ice chunks can engulf branches and resist unloading while also potentially altering turbulent energy exchanges by reducing wind flow compared to more porous snow clumps. A canopy ice reservoir could be added to better represent these processes. However, since this type of snow load was not observed in this research, this process could not be tested empirically and was thus not implemented. Moreover, investigations of the liquid water holding capacity of intercepted snow and vegetation elements could help the representation of refreezing of liquid water intercepted in the canopy.

Collection of subcanopy SWE over large spatial extents with aerial lidar derived subcanopy snow depths, and converted to SWE using observed or simulated snow densities such as in @Staines2023, have the potential to validate updates to the canopy snow interception and ablation parameterisations presented here over large spatial extents which could help further build confidence in these models. However, it will be important to consider the uncertainty in meteorological forcing which becomes more uncertain at larger extents away from station observations [e.g., @Tang2023] which will contribute to errors in simulated SWE in addition to the new parameterisations that represent snowfall partitioning by forest canopies. Moreover, accurately representing surface snowpack processes such as rain-on-snow, melt, sublimation, and wind redistribution will also play a role in achieving accurate simulations of observed subcanopy SWE.

The widespread application of these new algorithms at large scales will depend on the continued development of high-resolution (<10 m) global datasets of canopy coverage and height. Such datasets would serve multiple purposes: they could identify large canopy gaps—many times larger than the canopy height—where the relationship between leaf-contact area and hydrometeor trajectory angle breaks down and distinctive sets of energy and mass exchange processes occur [@Conway2018]. Additionally, information on individual tree species would enable parameterisation of likely species-dependent coefficients, further refining model accuracy. Beyond canopy characterization, the reliability of hydrological models and land-surface schemes depends fundamentally on robust meteorological forcing data, which is often downscaled to in-situ station observations [@Tang2023]. This underscores the critical importance of maintaining long-term hydrometeorological stations. Expanding the monitoring network to areas with limited current coverage—such as high-elevation and remote regions—would significantly improve the meteorological data that drives these modelling applications and, by extension, the quality of informed decision-making.

Future water resource studies and monitoring efforts in forested basins should directly consider forested areas, which have historically relied on transfer of SWE measurements from open sites to quantify water availability in forested basins [@Schneider2016; @Raleigh2025]. This approach has always been uncertain, and now with changing forest-snow hydrological regimes associated with climate and vegetation change are likely to become increasingly unsatisfactory. These process changes will affect the quantity, phase, and timing of snowfall, unloading, and meltwater reaching the ground, making open-site measurements less representative of total basin water storage. These findings emphasize the need to expand monitoring networks to include snow stations under forested canopies that accumulate significant snowpack, rather than relying solely on open-site locations. This is particularly critical in warmer regions, where forests play an increasingly important role in maintaining snow water equivalent by reducing subcanopy irradiance [@Pomeroy2009] that can extend snowpack persistence and reduces early-season melt losses.

The successful transferability of the new canopy snow interception and ablation parameterisations across diverse climate zones and forest types provides evidence of its robustness for application as a diagnostic tool for investigating impacts of needleleaf canopies on snow accumulation. When coupled with physically based hydrological models, this approach offers potential for advancing our understanding how these impacts will influence subsequent snowmelt runoff and downstream hydrology. Given that remote sensing of snow water equivalent in forested environments is expected to remain limited by the physical interference of forest canopies with electromagnetic radiation [@Rittger2020], this model-based diagnostic tool provides researchers with a valuable method for quantifying water stored as snow intercepted snow in forest canopies and on the forest floor and diagnosing future changes. However, it is important to emphasize that snowfall interception and partitioning by needleleaf canopies represents only one component of the hydrological cycle. Once precipitation reaches the ground, numerous other processes govern how much water ultimately contributes to runoff, including but not limited to subcanopy interception, evapotranspiration, surface snow melt, depressional storage, infiltration, subsurface storage, and transmission processes. Future research is also needed to help refine understanding of the aforementioned processes to improve the accuracy of hydrological models [e.g., @Groff2025]. The utility of hydrological models as diagnostic decision-making tools becomes increasingly important as climates warm and vegetation distributions shift. There is an urgent need to understand how these changes will affect snow accumulation in forests and subsequent runoff. Given the strong sensitivity of forest snow partitioning to canopy density and temperature—which govern melt, unloading, and sublimation processes—future changes in forest structure and climate are expected to significantly impact snow water storage. Using hydrological models as diagnostic tools can support decision-makers in developing informed strategies for diagnosing future water availability and the interactions with climate and vegetation as environmental conditions continue to evolve.
